sections.brief: Egypt's revolution as the stage's opening frame, July 1952–June 1956: the Free Officers' coup of 23 July 1952 (Nasser as leader, Naguib as figurehead, the 89 other officers per HISTORY.com, attributed), Farouk's removal, land reform, the republic of summer 1953, the 1954 contest with Naguib and the April decrees, the Heads of Agreement (27 July 1954) and the Suez base agreement of 19 October 1954 read from the FRUS note (1,200 technicians, the attack trigger covering Egypt, other Arab states and Turkey but not Iran or Israel, seven years, the 1888 Convention pledge), the Manshiya shooting of 26 October 1954, the Brotherhood ban and arrests, Naguib's removal in mid-November 1954, Nasser's request to the Soviet ambassador on 15 June 1954 (forward to cw2_czech_arms), and the 23 June 1956 presidency vote (99.95%, sole candidate). From me_s08 tell only Egypt 1952 (Syria 1949 is rd6's, Iran 1953 is cw1's s11, Suez and Iraq are later stages); from egi_src_s02 tell only Nasser's rise and Gaza under Egyptian administration to 1955, linking forward to Stage Three for Suez. Keep the Lavon operation to one forward sentence (it is lv_s01). Give Egyptian agency its full weight: the Free Officers' own aims, the Brotherhood's and Naguib's opposition, and say plainly that the Origins essay does not establish who ordered the Manshiya attempt. Figure: timeline July 1952–June 1956.

Picking up from Volume II's account of the border ([scene:rd6_return_barred|how return was barred], one linking sentence; do not retell its 2,700–5,000 or 90% figures), tell August–November 1953 in order: Unit 101's founding in August 1953 and merger into battalion 890 in January 1954 (Ministry of Defense archive), the al-Burj camp attack of late August 1953 (20 killed, per Morris via Khalidi and Caplan), the Yehud killing of a mother and two children on 12–13 October and the MAC's 'intolerable aggression' finding, the planning options and Dayan's authorization, the night of 14–15 October, the toll (present the 45/50 houses and 69/66 dead dispute), Sharon's later account, Ben-Gurion's 19 October broadcast denying any army role, Sharett's diary showing the settler story was a chosen cover and his 'Horror gripped me', the State Department's 18 October statement, and Resolution 101 (24 November 1953; 9–0–2, Lebanon and the USSR abstaining) in both its parts — the censure of Israel and the call on Jordan to stop crossings. Present Israel's case (attacks from across the line; the MAC's own finding on Yehud) and the case against (the Council, Washington, Sharett) with equal care, and examine the word 'retaliation' as each side used it. Figures: timeline August 1953–January 1954; key figures (69; 45; 9–0–2; 3 killed at Yehud).

The first time Washington held back aid to Israel, September 1953–January 1954: the works begun on 2 September 1953 in the Israel–Syria demilitarized zone (Eban's 'electric power project'), Bennike's request of 23 September, Sharett's reply and Syria's complaint, Dulles's decision to withhold Mutual Security funds on Byroade's advice, the 20 and 27 October press conferences (present the amount dispute: about $26 million released vs Dulles's recalled ~$100 million total vs the aide's $50–60 million, and say what each refers to), Resolution 100 of 27 October (unanimous, 'without prejudice'), the works stopped at midnight on 28 October, and Press Release 604 releasing the money. From sy_s02 tell only the 1953–56 demilitarized-zone dispute (Dayan's 'someone must keep the area alive', Syrian fire on farmers and fishermen, Israeli tractors), presenting both sides' conduct; leave the 1964–67 water war to Stage Six and Dayan's later 'at least 80 percent' to rd6's telling (one linking sentence). Show the mechanism: a UN officer's ruling, enforced by a US funding lever. Embed aid_arms:Leverage & Law:0 and aid_arms:Leverage & Law:1 and note that the dashboard's table begins in 1987 while this 1953 episode is an earlier documented case of a condition attached and met; map: syria_line. Figure: process flow (works begun → Bennike's request → aid withheld → Council resolution → works suspended → aid released).

The Johnston mission, October 1953–October 1955, as the diplomatic answer to Banat Yaacov: Eisenhower's 16 October 1953 statement (ambassadorial rank, refugees, 'mutual development'), the October 1953 telegram on the TVA/Main study and its political precondition (including Israel giving up exclusive control of the Lake Tiberias outlets), the Main, Cotton, Arab (1954) and Unified plans with their allocations (compare them in one table, noting AquaPedia's 394/393 inconsistency and Israel's 'residue' of about 409 mcm), the memoranda of 5 July and 11 October 1955, technical acceptance, and the Arab League's political refusal. Present the reasons for failure from both sides (recognition by implication; suspicion of benefit to Israel and Negev settlement; Iraqi and Saudi pressure) and Nasser's own advocacy; say plainly that the plan was never ratified but was broadly observed and later tied to US funding. Link [scene:sy_s02|the demilitarized zones] once. Figure: comparison table of the four plans (Israel, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon), sourced to AquaPedia and the State Department summary.

After the coup ([scene:s11|the coup of August 1953], one linking sentence): the oil settlement of October 1953–October 1954 in full, from ira_s00b and the primary record — Hoover's appointment (14 October 1953) and visit, Entezam's consortium proposal (1 November 1953), the 5 December 1953 communiqué, the 5 August 1954 agreement (AIOC 40%, Shell 14%, five US companies at 8% each named, the French 6% by arithmetic only), the £25 million compensation over ten years from 1957, the Senate's 41–4–3 vote on 28 October and the Shah's signature on 29 October 1954, and Hoover's 'significant victory'. Set ira_s00b's 'ended Iranian national control' beside the record: Entezam's 1953 proposal had the consortium buying from the National Iranian Oil Company, while the 1954 arrangements created foreign-held operating companies, incorporated in the Netherlands, for production and refining — give both, and the scene's claim that US companies entered Iranian oil for the first time. Tell SAVAK (1957) and the Mossad training claim only in a closing forward sentence: cw1 found that the sources fetched date the first Israeli–SAVAK contact to Bakhtiar's offer of September 1957, so ira_s00b's 'co-founding role' is for Stage Four to test, not stated here. Figure: money chain (Iranian oil → NIOC sale to the consortium → shares by company → who gained → the £25 million and what Iran gave up).

Israel's leadership split, July 1953–June 1956: Ben-Gurion's leave (7 July 1953), three-year security plan (18 October), resignation (7 December) and Sde Boker; the Sharett governments (26 January 1954–29 June 1955, then to 3 November 1955, noting the Prime Minister's Office listing's date problem); Ben-Gurion's return as defence minister on 21 February 1955 and as prime minister on 3 November 1955; Dulles's February 1955 defence-pact offer and the retaliation condition Israel would not accept; Sharett's resignation on 18 June 1956 and Ben-Gurion's 28 July letter. Use the diaries carefully: quote Sharett's and Dayan's dated words as translated, identify Rokach's 1980 study as an argued reading published by an Arab-American academic association, and set it against Caplan's and Shlaim's readings, each labelled. Present the strongest case for the activists in their own terms (deterrence after repeated killings across the line; no US guarantee on offer without a ban on retaliation) and for Sharett's restraint. Link to [scene:lv_s01|the Lavon affair] rather than retelling it. Figure: timeline July 1953–July 1956 of who held the premiership and defence ministry. Add the 26 July 1955 election (82.8% turnout; Mapai 40, Herut 15, General Zionists 13, National Religious Front 11, Ahdut HaAvoda 10, Mapam 9; the two Arab-list seats) and the three-month coalition talks that produced Ben-Gurion's 75-seat government of 3 November 1955; figure: key figures of the 1955 result.

The American home front, February 1954–July 1956, picking up from Stage One's account of the Knights of Columbus campaign ([scene:cw1_pledge|'Under God', 1951–53]): Docherty's sermon of 7 February 1954 with Eisenhower present and its Cold War language, the bills and the 14 June 1954 signing, Eisenhower's statement ('spiritual weapons'), the 1955 currency requirement, and H.J. Res. 396 / P.L. 84-851 of 30 July 1956 with the committee's 'spiritual and psychological value'. The statute record now settles the law numbers: the motto is P.L. 851 (ch. 795, 70 Stat. 732, 30 July 1956) and the currency act is No. 140 (H.R. 619, ch. 303, 11 July 1955); say HISTORY.com conflated them. State plainly that the documented motive was religious and anti-communist and that no source here links either change to Israel or to any Jewish or Zionist organization; any such reading would be interpretation and is not made. Figure: timeline February 1954–1957 (sermon, signing, currency law, motto law, first notes printed). Then answer the question a reader will ask, 'which God?', from cw2_pledge_which_god. The law says only 'God': no Trinity, no Christ, no named faith. Give the record for each reading side by side. The House report says the change establishes no religion. Eisenhower's 1952 line, 'and I don't care what it is', comes with his 'Judeo-Christian concept'. Docherty's own frame was 'the Christian ethic', and a reported paraphrase has him including Jews and Muslims; it is unconfirmed, so say so. O'Connor (2004) calls it a generic God, 'not under Jesus or Vishnu'. Explain that the working category in 1954 was 'Judeo-Christian', using Silk's history of that term and its later turn against Muslims. Note that 'Allah' is simply Arabic for God, used by Arab Christians and in Arabic Bibles: rejecting the word is not rejecting a different deity in the linguistic sense. Close with a section headed 'Reading the Architecture: Which God?', clearly marked as interpretation, never as finding. State the inference Ron draws from the pattern: in 1954 'God' was left unnamed six years after 1948, by a country whose former president called himself Cyrus in 1953, and which now gives Israel $3.8 billion a year. On that reading, the unnamed God is the God of Israel. Then lay out what supports it and what cuts against it, both sourced. Supports: the 'Judeo-Christian' frame; Truman's 'I am Cyrus' (November 1953); the Christian Zionist line from Scofield (link Volume II). Cuts against: the documented motive was anti-communism; the campaign was started by a Catholic order whose Church did not recognize Israel until 1993–94; aid was about $75 million a year then, against $3.8 billion under the 2016 MOU; and the same president who signed 'under God' forced Israel out of Sinai in 1957 under threat of sanctions (link cw3). Let the reader weigh it. Do not resolve it.

The year after Qibya, March 1954–January 1955, on three fronts. Jordan: the Scorpion Pass (Ma'ale Akrabim) killings of 17 March 1954 (eleven dead; the two wounded; the UN observer's count), the Mixed Armistice Commission's 2–2 vote with the chairman abstaining and his 'far from being conclusive', Israel's walk-out from 23 March and its 5 April complaint to the Council; then the Nahalin raid of 28–29 March (Jordan's 9 killed and 14 injured against the Commission's 5 National Guards, 1 woman and 3 soldiers; the footprints and Hebrew-marked ordnance; the 30 March condemnation, Israel absent). Present the Israeli case (an unanswered massacre of civilians) and the UN record with equal care, and keep the responsibility question open as the chairman did. Washington: Byroade's Dayton (9 or 19 April — give both dates) and Philadelphia (1 May) speeches, his words as Medoff quotes them, Eban's protest to Dulles and Israel's official protest, Neumann's 'Byroadeism'; tie the speeches to named officials and their stated reasoning, not to any group. Suez: the Bat Galim (seized 28 September 1954; Egypt's fishermen charge; the Commission's 19 November finding and the 25 November withdrawal of 'unfounded'; the crew's 94 days and release on 1 January 1955; the Council's January 1955 affirmation that Resolution 95 kept 'continuing validity and effect'), linking back to [scene:cw1_suez_blockade|the 1951 resolution]. Figure: timeline March 1954–January 1955; key figures (11 killed; 2–2–1; 9 or 8 killed at Nahalin; 10 crew; 94 days).

Operation Susannah and the first round of 'the Affair', June 1954–February 1955, in full from lv_s01 and the research: Unit 131 under Ben-Zur; the aim (to damage Egypt's ties with the West during the Suez base talks, blame to fall on the Brotherhood, Communists or 'local nationalists'); the dated sequence from Raseef22's Egyptian-sourced account (16 June signal, 2 July, 14 July, 23 July) attributed as such; Natanson's arrest; the eleven arrests, the trial (11 December 1954–27 January 1955), the sentences by name, the executions of Marzouk and Azar on 31 January 1955, Max Bennett's death in custody, Avri Elad; Lavon's denial vs Gibli's claim vs Dayan's blame, the two-man inquiry, Lavon's resignation and Ben-Gurion's return. Present the casualty conflict (none per Ynet and the Jewish Press vs deaths per Raseef22; no primary record found, so it stays open) and the order dispute without resolving either. Say who paid: the Egyptian Jewish operatives, executed and imprisoned, and Israel's 2005 recognition (Katsav; Kimche's 'never to go down that road again'); link [scene:s00e2|the Jews of the Arab world] for the community's fate rather than retelling it. Treat lv_s01's 'earliest documented false flag' as the scene's characterization, not a sourced superlative, and do not use it as a finding. Decision for this stage: the 1960–61 reopening (forged documents, the committee of seven, Ben-Gurion's 1963 resignation) is told in Stage Four; close with one forward sentence. Figure: timeline June 1954–February 1955; comparison of the three accounts of who gave the order.

The intelligence relationship, 1954–1956, picking up from Stage One's three accounts of its start ([scene:cw1_cia_liaison|the liaison's origins]): Angleton's appointment to head the new Counterintelligence Staff in 1954 and his control of the Israel account as 'an administrative anomaly' (CIA historian), his view of Israel as 'a bastion against the Soviet Union', then the Khrushchev speech (February 1956; Grayevsky, Barmor, Dorot; Dulles by mid-April; The New York Times in early June), attributing each step to its source and noting the Mossad/Shin Bet discrepancy. From cia_s03 tell only the 1954 start and the 'gentleman's agreement' as Ambassador Lewis later described it (his words, dated to his 1977–85 service); NUMEC, LAKAM and Pollard belong to Stages Four to Six and later volumes — one forward sentence linking [scene:df_s04|the CIA–Mossad liaison], whose discipline that a shared hub is not a pipeline applies here. State that no formal written agreement for 1954–56 is documented in these sources. Figure: process flow of the speech's route (Warsaw → Shin Bet → Jerusalem → Washington liaison → CIA → publication).

The Anglo-American search for a settlement, December 1954–March 1956: Alpha's start (Russell and Shuckburgh, 20 December 1954), its terms (Negev land link, 75,000 refugees, non-belligerence), Dulles's address of 26 August 1955 read closely (900,000 refugees; 'resettlement and, to such an extent as may be feasible, repatriation'; compensation due from Israel with a US-backed loan; a treaty guarantee of agreed borders; Jerusalem; water), the 1 September reassurances to Nasser and Fawzi's dismissal, the Anderson mission (January–March 1956) and Eisenhower's letters of 27 February. Present how each side received it from the sources (Egyptian refusal to engage; Israel's refusal to cede territory and its wish for arms and a guarantee instead), and say plainly that the record fetched does not settle whether either leader could have accepted. Figure: comparison of Dulles's proposals and each side's documented position (refugees, borders, guarantee, Jerusalem). Add Eden's speech of 9 November 1955 (call it the Mansion House speech, as the US Embassy did, and note it is also known as the Guildhall speech): 'some compromise between these two positions', Dulles's 'US is in no sense committed', Eytan's objections and Ben-Gurion's 'truncate Israel' reply of 15 November.

The region choosing sides, February 1955–October 1956: the Baghdad Pact read from its text (24 February 1955; Articles 1, 5 and 7) and the accession dates, why Washington stayed out (the November 1956 position paper: Israel's guarantee demand, Senate ratification, Arab rivalries, Moscow) while joining committees and paying $76,350; Bandung (18–24 April 1955; 29 states; Nasser's emergence; Israel not invited despite U Nu and Nehru, with Indonesia's opposition; the communiqué's 'rights of the Arab people of Palestine'; Haj Amin al-Husseini in Yemen's delegation); then Jordan: the December 1955 Majali crisis and riots, Glubb's dismissal (1–2 March 1956) with the Amman report's reasons, the Arab Legion's Arabization, and the 21 October 1956 Nabulsi victory. Keep each state's decision tied to named governments and leaders; show convergence, not conspiracy (British base interests, Iraqi Hashemite aims, Egyptian opposition, US hesitation). Link Turkey's later secret pact forward to Stage Four ([scene:tk_s03|Turkey and Israel]). Figure: power structure of the Pact in 1956 (members, the US as non-member participant, Egypt and Saudi Arabia opposed).

The Gaza raid and what followed, February–September 1955: the Israeli case for the raid (the border incidents and the killing that preceded it, per the Defense Ministry archive), the night of 28 February, the casualty figures by source (38 and 8; 37 soldiers and 2 civilians; 38 and 31 or 33 wounded — present all), the MAC finding of 6 March and Resolution 106 (29 March, unanimous); Gaza's own response — the 1 March demonstration, Hosni Belal's death, the communist–Brotherhood committee, the demands (end the Sinai resettlement scheme of 12,000 families; arms for the camps), the arrests of 8–9 March — as Palestinian political agency in its own right; then the fedayeen (Battalion 141 under Mustafa Hafez from September 1955 to his killing in July 1956), linking back to rd6 for Nasser's 31 August announcement ([scene:rd6_return_barred|the infiltration years]). Present the dispute over consequences with each side's evidence: Shlaim and Allen (the raid pushed Egypt toward Soviet arms) against Eban (the Baghdad Pact did) and the Soviet record of Nasser's arms request of 15 June 1954. Figures: key figures (38; 8; 37 + 2; 12,000 families); timeline 28 February–September 1955. Add the late-summer escalation: Burns's report of 22 August (an Egyptian officer and two soldiers killed) and the eleven killed inside Israel in the attacks that followed; Israel's 31 August letter (four civilians killed near Kfar Menahem); and the Khan Yunis raid of 31 August–1 September 1955 with both counts (36 killed and 13 wounded per UNTSO; 10 soldiers and 25 refugees killed and 19 injured per Egypt). A figure of 72 dead circulates from secondary works and has not been verified; leave it out.

The arms race, June 1954–September 1956: Nasser's 1954 request to Moscow (one sentence, back-link to cw2_free_officers), the announcement of 27 September 1955 (tanks, MiG-15s, bombers; 'more than $83 million', attributed; 'unconditional'), the payment in cotton and rice and the £1 million on account, Allen's account of why US arms talks had stalled (the military-mission requirement); Israel's response — Eban's request of 16 November 1955, Sharett's December plea and the twelve Mystères held up for US approval, the postponement of 13 December after the Kinneret raid, the final US refusal in April 1956 — and the French channel (Peres; Shlaim's reading of French and American motives, labelled), ending with the State Department's September 1956 estimate of 24 or possibly 48 Mystères and France's offer of 24 more. Embed aid_arms:Overview:2 and discuss its first step (economic aid and loans only, 1948–1961, avoiding arms sales for fear of alienating Arab oil states) as the policy behind the refusals. Convergence, not conspiracy: show who in Washington, Paris and Jerusalem wanted what. Figure: timeline June 1954–September 1956 of arms requests and deliveries.

The border and the United Nations, December 1955–October 1956: the Kinneret raid of 11–12 December 1955 (Shlaim on Ben-Gurion's sole authorization and Sharett's and Eban's reactions; UNTSO's 'striking disparity'; the US Embassy's 'severe blunder'), Resolution 111 (19 January 1956, unanimous; 'flagrant violation'; Syrian interference 'in no way justifies'; the warning of further measures), Hammarskjöld's mission (4 April resolution; 10 April–3 May; the 9 May report and the conditional assurances), the 4 June resolution, the August 1956 killings on both sides of the Gaza line, and Qalqilya (10–11 October 1956; 'heavy casualties', no figure in the Yearbook). Present Israel's case (Syrian fire on fishermen; mines and ambushes) and the Council's at full strength, and keep Kafr Qasim and Sinai for Stage Three with one forward sentence. Figure: timeline December 1955–October 1956.

From the dam to the Canal, December 1955–26 July 1956, ending the stage: the 16 December 1955 offer (Hart's recollection of $56 million at once and the 85/15 split, labelled as recollection; the conditions and Nasser's objection), the morning decision of 19 July 1956 with its reasons, the afternoon meeting with Ambassador Hussein (cost $1.3 billion, 'put on the shelf', 'hostile to us'; Hussein on the Soviet offer), the dispute over why (the documented reasons; Bowie's and Wilkins's account of Congress, naming cotton growers, Israel's supporters and the China lobby as constituencies, not as a single hand; Hart's 'impulsive'; Cortada's 'trap'), and the nationalization of 26 July with the offer of compensation. Give Egypt's case at full strength (sovereignty, the population argument). Link forward to Stage Three for Sèvres and the war, and to egi_src_s02 there. Figure: timeline December 1955–26 July 1956; comparison of the reasons given for the withdrawal by source.

Closing synthesis: the architecture as it stood on 26 July 1956. In one section, show how the stage's threads joined — retaliation as policy (Unit 101 to Qalqilya) and the Council's censures; Washington's levers and limits (the 1953 aid suspension, the Johnston plan, Alpha, the refusal of arms, the Aswan withdrawal); the Soviet-bloc entry through Czech arms; France as the alternative supplier; the Baghdad Pact and Bandung as rival alignments; Egypt's consolidation under Nasser; the intelligence channel through Angleton; Iran's oil settled in Western hands; and the American home front's anti-communist piety (with no documented Israel link). Name, for each, the power that acted, its interest, and who opposed it inside the same government (Sharett vs Ben-Gurion; State vs Congress; Hart vs Dulles). Use only facts from the stage's own sections and research. Figure: the chapter's synthesis power-structure diagram (Washington, London, Paris, Moscow/Prague; Israel; Egypt; Jordan, Syria, Iraq; the UN), with each tie labelled by its documented type.
